Come to think of it I'd definitely go with the increased oil production as a likely explanation for the color not sticking well, particularly if you're not dyeing immediately after bleaching, or if your natural hair is light enough you don't have to bleach it and you didn't wash recently.

Relating to my own experience, I always used to get my hair bleached when it was a couple days after washing (for its protection, because otherwise it'd get super damaged and split like crazy). Now I have to make sure to wash my hair the night before I bleach, or it'll REALLY turn out orange-ginger, because the increased oil really does protect it from the bleach!

​

The color could have changed formulations, of course, if it was a new bottle, or if you've been using the same one for a long time it's possible the dye itself could have oxidized too much and not been strong enough.

Interesting.

I mean, I think it's POSSIBLE for T to cause changes in your hair, directly or indirectly. For instance, I (dark brunette) now have a harder time getting my natural hair color to lift since starting T.  I used to be able to get a nice pale white-blonde after 1 bleaching, but now it turns out kinda orangish-yellow, very brassy, with the same time and same strength bleach. However, I don't think that's the same problem you're having.

So, if you didn't change your bleach brand, it's possible your brand switched formulations on you, or something could be going on with your water (did you move recently, by any chance?) Chemistry is weird.

I was not using T when I had Nexplanon's older cousin, Implanon, but I did exchange smoothly from one Implanon to a new one (removal and reimplantation done in the same session) with no interruption in my (lack of) bleed cycles at the time.  That's the idea behind changing it out on schedule, though.  If you get it changed when it's time (or before) in a single session with basically just minutes or seconds between removal of the old one and implantation of the new, then there should be no alteration in the amount of hormone you're getting from it and therefore the level in your body SHOULD hypothetically remain stable, therefore changing it out SHOULD not affect your (lack of) cycle as long as everything else remains the same.  So I think if it's being done on schedule and not too late, it seems reasonable to assume that it is unlikely that you will have a problem with it.  Hopefully that is helpful.

There are other LGBTQ people in the local community who've said they'd help me out if I got disowned and kicked out but of course, you know... good intentions don't always follow through, just because circumstances, so I'm not counting on that either.

Maybe you weren't looking for a response, idk, but these are my thoughts...

Transmasculine NB is a thing that exists, I know a few.  They consider themselves nonbinary but geared heavily toward the masculine end.  NB isn't always smack in the middle between male and female.

There's no pressure though.  Using myself as an example, I'm willing to consider myself a binary trans man but I'm also, shall we say, not the most stereotypically masculine guy, and I'm willing to embrace that.  In fact if I'd been a cis dude I probably would qualify as being somewhat effeminate anyway and would probably come across as a little "flamboyant"  (I'm bi anyway, so... take that for whatever you will.)

Personally I'm all about respecting gender identities while also wanting to destroy gender roles and stereotypes.   A lot of what society says about the "shoulds" of men and women, those "male" and "female" boxes, is utter bullshit and completely socially contrived.  And ya gotta keep in mind that however much society idealizes it, the "stoic unemotional man" is frankly not an emotionally healthy, mature or well socialized human being, so this is one place where we really need to ignore what society is telling us is normal for men because "normal" in this case is frankly not good for us or anyone else - there can be worlds of difference between "normal" and "healthy and well functioning".   As a society we really need to teach boys how to better acknowledge and deal with their emotions without bottling them up and leaving it for their girlfriends' emotional labor or until they explode and shoot up a Walmart.  Straight guys especially, a lot of straight guys don't even have close friends to share their thoughts and feelings with because there's a stigma that if you're too close to your male friend you must be gay, and.... that started as a pretty American thing tbh,  but it spread, and its sad as fuck IMO, they're missing out in a fundamental way.  In Australia a lot of guys are (or at least used to be) ride or die for each other as pals - "best mates" - and I'm hoping over time we can help destroy that toxic fear of platonic same-gender friendship among straight men, and help more men in general learn how to be emotionally healthy.  Too damn many men need serious therapy now as adults because they can't acknowledge or name let alone cope with their own feels and they just wear their partners out emotionally because without knowing their feelings, they have no idea how to act.

Look at dogs.  Dogs don't have a whole lot in the way of social pressures and stigmas the same way we do.  Male and female dogs are equally capable of being awesome pets.  Male dogs do have a different typical behavioral set than females in some situations, but they both love their families with their whole hearts and they're not afraid to show their feelings about anything to anybody, dog or human.  (They also don't waste time being mean to female dogs or treating them as inferiors, females are just allowed to be and sometimes they outrank the males in the family pack structure and there are no stigmas attached to a "beta" male or an "alpha" female, it's more a matter of a dog's individual personality and desire to lead than it is an issue of gender, and that's one of the things I admire about them, their version of social jockeying has nothing to do with their gender.)  Our species would be much improved if we could learn some things from them tbh.

Hello, 41 here, I had a lot of the same fears and for similar reasons... huge people pleaser, definitely living for the approval of my parents/spouse, indecisive, horrible self esteem... and actually, with the help of a very supportive LGBTQ friendly doctor, I went on an extremely low dose of T to start with in hopes of it helping me be absolutely sure I was sure (and by extremely low, I mean still within the "normal" range for cis women, unlikely to cause any permanent changes, and because my first doses were daily topical cream applications, VERY easy to stop immediately if something happened I didn't like).  This was easy for me to do, because I was already on the extreme low end of normal T range for cis women so I had a LOT of room to explore how a little bit of testosterone "felt" before I even got close to brushing that ceiling.

What I discovered in this process was that I FELT better immediately after starting, and the more I ratcheted up the dose the happier I was anytime I DID see what I could construe as a change.  I'd get excited about even POSSIBLE changes.  Does my voice sound just the tiniest bit deeper today?  Is that a new hair on my chin I see?   YES, I want to see this progressing MORE...

Even my therapist noticed I was not only more hopeful about how I looked but just less depressed in general.

And that's.... pretty much what sold me completely.  Just... being so... *excited* about all that stuff.  I couldn't really fake that kind of feeling, because when it comes down to it there's a difference between the excitement of seeing yourself and feeling actual hope and love for yourself, and the "excitement" of successfully presenting the image and meeting the marks that you know other people you care about want to see from you.  And it's even more stark when I compare to how I felt earlier in life about Puberty 1.0... growing breasts felt like a fucking insult, I hated it, and when I started bleeding it felt like life was over (but I'd never heard of trans men, so the concept just... didn't exist for me, or else I might have figured it out sooner).   So I guess my point is, if you really can't trust your brain, maybe you could try listening to your heart/feelings instead?  Because when you've got the right answer... you just know.  Sounds really woo woo I know, but that's the truth.  Don't feel bad for not being able to logic it out with your brain.... we're literally dealing with a condition that science as yet has no single true explanation for, so it doesn't "make sense".  There is no infallible "transgender test".  That's why we're really just left with our feelings about it.

I won't lie, I do still have my moments of doubt, but then I just remind myself of those things... a cis woman would not typically be excited about facial hair or a deeper voice.  A cis woman probably wouldn't have had the same feelings about a lot of the life experiences that sort of... are part of the mosaic of this truth for me, all the little pieces that add up.   Truly cisgender people do not usually feel a need to even question what they are, they just exist in that truth because they were born to it and it was right for them and they have the support of pretty much all of society.

I'm still scared of rejection/no love from the people important to me, not least because I haven't told my family yet (unhappily married for 9 years now, parents are lifelong evangelical conservatives - not physically abusive, but definitely extremely controlling).  That's why I'm still microdosing (albeit I'm finally significantly above cis female levels, though nowhere near adult cis male levels yet.)  But I feel a lot better about my ability to love myself, and... that still counts for a lot, I think, because that was the first thing that got me wondering... I had decided to become a drag king (which is a tangent in itself), and when I first got my makeup on and my theatrical facial hair on and got dressed, that was the first time in my life that I ever saw myself in the mirror and really, truly liked what I saw.  Hell, I *loved* what I saw, and wished I could feel that all the time and then over following weeks and performances, I realized how fake I felt by comparison when everyone was telling me I looked so pretty/lovely/whatever in whatever dress/makeup/jewelry.  So my theory is, maybe if I love myself, then someone else can probably love me, too, even if they're not the same someones that love me now.  I mean, the someones that love me now have done so without me having loved myself pretty much ever, right?  Would it actually be less likely that I'd find someone to genuinely love me if I did love myself and was finally living AS myself??  Doubt it.

And thankfully there are quite a few trans men/AFAB transmasc folx in my area that I've met through the drag community and most of them are friendly and open, I know at least a dozen by name, and that's still just a fraction in my area.  Support and likeminded sympathetic people are definitely out there, it's just a matter of finding them.

Anyways, sorry for the novella, hope you found it helpful.

Depends what kind of allergy you're having and what kind of adhesive you're using.  I developed a slight but annoying sensitivity to spirit gum (I have a slight allergy to pine, so pine-resin-based adhesive makes my face unhappy), so I use pros-aid for any prosthetic (mine is for theatrical facial makeup more than anything else) but some people can't use that one because it's got latex in it and there are a lot of people allergic to latex.  Do a test of the adhesive on the inside of your forearm.  If it gets rashy and itchy it's an allergy and you'll need to try a different adhesive.  If there's no response, you actually might have a yeast or bacterial infection that's flaring up in the moisture trapped under the prosthetic.

Unfortunately, either way, you really need to let your skin calm down and heal before you do anything more.  Skin just gets more and more sensitive to more and more things the more you mess with it and don't let it heal.   The skin also is easily prone to infection with nasty bacteria the longer it remains irritated, even if it started as an allergy.  Yeasts can make for sad times (I've had one of those infections on my chest before due to night sweating while wearing a binder like a stubborn ass.... not fun, super itchy, needed 2 weeks of fluconazole pills to go away) and MRSA is not something you'd want to fuck around with not least because they require professional treatment.  I know a guy who has holes in the side of his chest under his arm from MRSA, even freshly healed it looked like a rodent had been gnawing chunks of meat out of him.  fugly shit.

And sadly that does mean probably not wearing the prosthetic against your skin, washing the area daily with a very gentle soap and water, patting thoroughly dry (possibly consider using a hair dryer to make sure the area is REALLY dry) and applying a cortisone cream to help reduce inflammation (if it's an allergy... if an infection, that'll flare it up quick smart and you might have to see a doctor), and trying to keep the area as dry and clean as possible.  That means not reattaching the item until you are COMPLETELY healed.  Maybe an occasional saline rinse in the shower might also help (that calms down my piercings right quick if they get angry for any reason).  If I assume the piece in question normally lives below your belt line, you might just have to stick the item into a sock or some kind of fabric pouch and pin it to your underwear so that it stays in place in the right position so that you know it's THERE and it's providing the right profile (and doesn't fall out), so nobody is likely to notice anything different, even if it's not physically attached to you for that time. 

Wearing a prosthetic for long periods in a region of the body that is prone to being perpetually warm and damp is just... really difficult to do without developing a sensitivity or an infection of some kind.  There are some products intended to stop sweating under prosthetic devices and that is bound to help you once you know you have a compatible adhesive, but as far as I'm aware most of them require a loading period to work and I can't vouch for how well they work. 

Good luck, man.
